### **Women's Shot Put Competition Prediction & Preview**  

#### **Predicted Finish & Marks:**  
1. **Sarah Mitton (CAN)** – **20.45m**  
2. **Chase Jackson (USA)** – **20.20m**  
3. **Jessica Schilder (NED)** – **19.95m**  
4. **Maddison-Lee Wesche (NZL)** – **19.70m**  
5. **Jaida Ross (USA)** – **19.50m**  
6. **Jiayuan Song (CHN)** – **19.30m**  
7. **Danniel Thomas-Dodd (JAM)** – **19.10m**  
8. **Maggie Ewen (USA)** – **18.90m**  
9. **Fanny Roos (SWE)** – **18.60m**  
10. **Jessica Inchude (POR)** – **18.40m**  

---  

### **Reasoning & Analysis**  

#### **1. Sarah Mitton (CAN) – 20.45m**  
Mitton has been the most consistent performer in 2024-25, with multiple 20m+ throws, including a **20.68m** win in Fleetwood (May 2024) and a **20.48m** win in Nanjing (March 2025). She also won the Paris Olympics (19.77m) and Brussels Diamond League (20.25m). Her ability to peak in big competitions and recent indoor dominance (20.68m in Karlsruhe) suggests she’s in the best form right now.  

#### **2. Chase Jackson (USA) – 20.20m**  
Jackson has the highest ceiling (20.64m in Lausanne, 20.10m in Eugene) but has been inconsistent, with a **17.60m disaster in Paris** and a **19.43m in Val-de-Reuil**. She’s a big-meet performer (2022 & 2023 World Champion), but Mitton has been more reliable lately.  

#### **3. Jessica Schilder (NED) – 19.95m**  
Schilder is on a **hot streak in 2025**, with a **20.69m indoor PB** in Apeldoorn and a **20.47m outdoor win in Xiamen**. She’s younger (25) and improving rapidly, but her inconsistency (17.81m in Suzhou 2024) keeps her just behind the top two.  

#### **4. Maddison-Lee Wesche (NZL) – 19.70m**  
Wesche is a **big-game performer** (Olympic silver in 2024) and has thrown **19.86m in Paris** and **19.81m in Schönebeck**. She struggles in weaker meets (16.52m in Nanjing 2025) but tends to show up when it counts.  

#### **5. Jaida Ross (USA) – 19.50m**  
Ross is a rising star (first collegiate woman over 20m) but hasn’t replicated that form in pro meets. Her best is **20.01m in Fayetteville (2024)** but she’s been **inconsistent (17.65m in Xiamen 2025)**. Still, she has the talent to challenge for a top-5 spot.  

#### **6. Jiayuan Song (CHN) – 19.30m**  
Song has **peaked well in China (19.83m in Suzhou 2024)** but struggles abroad (17.92m in Xiamen 2025). She’s a solid mid-tier thrower but lacks the consistency to break into the top 5.  

#### **7. Danniel Thomas-Dodd (JAM) – 19.10m**  
Thomas-Dodd is past her prime (32 years old) and hasn’t hit 19.50m+ since 2023. Her best in 2025 is **18.80m in Miramar**, and she’s been **inconsistent (17.48m in Paris 2024)**.  

#### **8. Maggie Ewen (USA) – 18.90m**  
Ewen is **more of a hammer thrower** and has been **inconsistent in shot put (NM in Loughborough, 17.74m in Berlin 2024)**. Her best in 2025 is **19.25m in Miramar**, but she’s not a medal threat.  

#### **9. Fanny Roos (SWE) – 18.60m**  
Roos has **struggled to break 19m consistently** in 2025 (best: **19.11m in Apeldoorn**). She’s a solid thrower but lacks the power to compete with the top group.  

#### **10. Jessica Inchude (POR) – 18.40m**  
Inchude has **peaked at 19.21m (Nicosia 2025)** but is usually in the **18.00-18.50m range**. She’s improved but still the weakest in this field.  

---  

### **Final Thoughts**  
- **Mitton** is the favorite based on **recent dominance and consistency**.  
- **Jackson** has the **highest upside** but is too inconsistent to trust for gold.  
- **Schilder** is the **dark horse**, trending upward with massive indoor throws.  
- **Wesche & Ross** could surprise if they hit big, but **Song & Thomas-Dodd** are fading.  
- **Ewen, Roos, Inchude** are **fighting for minor placements**.  

This should be a **tight battle between Mitton and Jackson**, but **Schilder could steal silver if Jackson underperforms**.

### **Men's Pole Vault Competition Prediction & Preview**  

#### **Predicted Final Standings & Marks:**  
1. **Armand Duplantis (SWE)** – **6.15m**  
2. **Emmanouil Karalis (GRE)** – **6.00m**  
3. **Sam Kendricks (USA)** – **5.95m**  
4. **Ernest John Obiena (PHI)** – **5.90m**  
5. **Kurtis Marschall (AUS)** – **5.85m**  
6. **Menno Vloon (NED)** – **5.82m**  
7. **Ersu Şaşma (TUR)** – **5.80m**  
8. **Ben Broeders (BEL)** – **5.72m**  
9. **Sondre Guttormsen (NOR)** – **5.70m**  
10. **Bokai Huang (CHN)** – **5.60m**  
11. **Chenyang Li (CHN)** – **5.50m**  

---  

### **Reasoning & Analysis**  

#### **1. Armand Duplantis (SWE) – 6.15m**  
- **Why 1st?** The undisputed GOAT of pole vaulting. His recent form is unmatched, with **five 6.00m+ clearances in 2025 alone**, including a **6.27m world record** in February. Even on an "off" day, he clears **6.10m+** with ease.  
- **Standout Results:**  
  - **6.26m (2024), 6.25m (2024), 6.27m (2025)** – consistently the highest vaulter in the world.  
  - **6.10m+ in 7 of his last 10 competitions** – no one else is even close.  
- **Weakness?** None. He could win even if he has a bad day.  

#### **2. Emmanouil Karalis (GRE) – 6.00m**  
- **Why 2nd?** The **most improved** vaulter in 2025. He has **three 6.00m+ jumps this year**, including a **6.05m** in Nanjing. His consistency is rising, and he’s now a legitimate threat to challenge Duplantis on a great day.  
- **Standout Results:**  
  - **6.01m (indoor, 2025), 6.02m (indoor, 2025), 6.05m (indoor, 2025)** – proving he can hit big heights.  
  - **Beat Kendricks in Berlin (5.94m to 5.85m)** – showing he can outperform veterans.  
- **Weakness?** Still lacks Duplantis' consistency at 6.10m+, but he’s closing the gap.  

#### **3. Sam Kendricks (USA) – 5.95m**  
- **Why 3rd?** A **proven championship performer**, but his peak is slightly declining. He’s still **regularly over 5.90m**, but he hasn’t hit 6.00m since **2024**.  
- **Standout Results:**  
  - **6.01m (2024)** – his last big jump.  
  - **Multiple 5.90m+ clearances** – but often loses to Duplantis and now Karalis.  
- **Weakness?** Age (32) is starting to show. He’s still elite, but not the **6.06m** vaulter he once was.  

#### **4. Ernest John Obiena (PHI) – 5.90m**  
- **Why 4th?** A **strong technician**, but his **consistency is shaky**. He has **5.90m+ ability**, but he often falters in big fields.  
- **Standout Results:**  
  - **5.97m (2024)** – his best recent jump.  
  - **Struggles in stacked fields (5.65m in Glasgow, 5.70m in Stockholm)** – can’t always deliver under pressure.  
- **Weakness?** Inconsistent in deep competitions.  

#### **5. Kurtis Marschall (AUS) – 5.85m**  
- **Why 5th?** A **solid performer**, but not quite at the **5.90m+ elite level** yet. He’s had **5.90m jumps**, but not recently.  
- **Standout Results:**  
  - **5.91m (2025 indoor)** – shows potential.  
  - **Often 5.80m-5.85m** – just below the top tier.  
- **Weakness?** Struggles to break into the **5.95m+** range consistently.  

#### **6. Menno Vloon (NED) – 5.82m**  
- **Why 6th?** A **decent vaulter**, but **not a medal threat**. He’s **consistent around 5.80m**, but rarely higher.  
- **Standout Results:**  
  - **5.92m (2024)** – his best recent jump.  
  - **Often 5.70m-5.80m** – lacks the extra gear.  
- **Weakness?** Doesn’t have the upside of Karalis or Kendricks.  

#### **7. Ersu Şaşma (TUR) – 5.80m**  
- **Why 7th?** **Inconsistent**. He’s had **5.90m jumps**, but also **many failures at lower heights**.  
- **Standout Results:**  
  - **5.90m (2025 indoor)** – shows potential.  
  - **Often no-heights or sub-5.70m** – unreliable.  
- **Weakness?** Too hit-or-miss.  

#### **8-11: The Rest**  
- **Ben Broeders (BEL) – 5.72m** – **Solid but unspectacular**.  
- **Sondre Guttormsen (NOR) – 5.70m** – **Struggling for form in 2025**.  
- **Bokai Huang (CHN) – 5.60m** – **Decent domestically, but not world-class**.  
- **Chenyang Li (CHN) – 5.50m** – **Still developing**.  

---  

### **Final Thoughts**  
- **Duplantis wins easily** unless he has a rare off day.  
- **Karalis is the rising star** and could push for **6.00m+**.  
- **Kendricks is still a podium threat**, but age is catching up.  
- **Obiena & Marschall** are **just outside the medals**.  
- **The rest are fighting for minor places**.  

**Predicted Winning Jump:** **6.15m (Duplantis)**, with **Karalis as the dark horse**.

### **Men's 400m Hurdles – Race Prediction & Preview**  

#### **Predicted Finish & Times:**  
1. **Karsten Warholm (NOR)** – **46.85**  
2. **Kyron McMaster (IVB)** – **47.12**  
3. **Matheus Lima (BRA)** – **47.45**  
4. **CJ Allen (USA)** – **47.78**

6. **Berke Akçam (TUR)** – **48.30**

8. **Gerald Drummond (CRC)** – **48.90**  
9. **Zhiyu Xie (CHN)** – **49.50**  

---  

### **Race Analysis & Reasoning:**  

#### **1. Karsten Warholm (NOR) – 46.85**  
Warholm is the clear favorite. Despite being 28, he remains the world record holder (45.94) and has shown consistent sub-47 form in recent years. His **46.95 in Chorzów (Aug 2024)** and **46.70 in Oslo (May 2024)** prove he’s still elite. His **300m hurdles time of 33.05 (April 2025)** is the fastest ever, showing his raw speed hasn’t declined. His only recent losses were to Rai Benjamin (not in this race), so he should dominate here.  

#### **2. Kyron McMaster (IVB) – 47.12**  
McMaster is the second-best in this field. His **48.05 in Stockholm (June 2024)** and **47.79 in Paris (Aug 2024)** show he’s in strong form. He’s a **silver medalist at the 2023 Worlds** and has run **47.08 (PB)**—only Warholm and Benjamin have gone faster. His **48.15 win in Paris (Aug 2024)** shows he can handle pressure. However, he lacks Warholm’s explosiveness, so he’ll likely finish a strong second.  

#### **3. Matheus Lima (BRA) – 47.45**  
Lima is the rising star. His **48.12 in Chorzów (Aug 2024)** and **33.98 in the 300m hurdles (April 2025, second only to Warholm)** suggest he’s improving rapidly. His **44.52 flat 400m speed** is the fastest in this field, meaning his hurdle endurance is the only question. If he executes cleanly, he could challenge McMaster.  

#### **4. CJ Allen (USA) – 47.78**  
Allen has been inconsistent but has **sub-48 potential (47.81 in Eugene, June 2024)**. His **48.16 in Stockholm (June 2024)** and **48.20 in Zürich (Sep 2024)** show he’s competitive, but he lacks the big-race pedigree of Warholm/McMaster. His **46.44 flat 400m** is strong, but his hurdle technique isn’t as refined.  

#### **5. Carl Bengtström (SWE) – 48.05**  
Bengtström is a solid European-level hurdler but hasn’t broken into the world elite. His **47.36 flat 400m (June 2024)** is impressive, but his **48.42 in Borås (Aug 2024)** suggests he’s plateauing. He’s consistent but lacks the closing speed to challenge the top three.  

#### **6. Berke Akçam (TUR) – 48.30**  
Akçam is young and improving, with a **48.14 in Rome (June 2024)** and **48.58 in Chorzów (Aug 2024)**. However, he’s inconsistent—his **49.48 in Paris (Aug 2024)** was mediocre. His **46.48 flat 400m** is decent, but he’s not yet at the level of Lima or Allen.  

#### **7. Nick Smidt (NED) – 48.55**  
Smidt is a solid technician but lacks elite speed. His **48.36 in Borås (Aug 2024)** is respectable, but his **49.43 in Rome (June 2024)** shows inconsistency. His **PB is only 49.28**, so he’s unlikely to challenge for top 5.  

#### **8. Gerald Drummond (CRC) – 48.90**  
Drummond has regressed in 2024-25. His **48.56 in Eugene (May 2024)** was decent, but his **49.63 in Brussels (Sep 2024)** and **35.61 in the 300m hurdles (April 2025)** suggest he’s past his peak.  

#### **9. Zhiyu Xie (CHN) – 49.50**  
Xie is the weakest here. His **49.40 in Quzhou (Sep 2024)** is his best recent time, and his **34.95 in the 300m hurdles (April 2025)** is well behind the field. He’s not yet at world-class level.  

---  

### **Final Thoughts:**  
- **Warholm** wins comfortably unless he makes a major error.  
- **McMaster** is the safest bet for silver, but **Lima** could surprise if he runs a perfect race.  
- **Allen and Bengtström** will battle for 4th, with **Akçam** just behind.  
- **Smidt, Drummond, and Xie** are fighting to avoid last place.  

This race will likely be decided by **Warholm’s dominance, McMaster’s consistency, and Lima’s breakthrough potential.** Everyone else is fighting for scraps.

Expect a fast race, but not a world record—**12:42 is realistic for Aregawi**.

His **raw speed** is unmatched right now—his **9.77 (+0.9)** in Kingston last year is the **fastest legal time** among this field in recent years.  
- **Recent Form:** His **6.48 (-2.1!)** in January 2025 shows he’s still in **elite shape** despite wind resistance. He thrives in **championship races**, and his **explosive start + top-end speed** make him the favorite.

- **Why 5th?** Tebogo is **more of a 200m specialist** (Olympic gold in 2024), and his **100m is inconsistent**. His **9.87 in Rome** was great, but **10.20 in Xiamen** suggests he’s **not fully focused** on the shorter sprint.  
- **Potential:** If he **committed to the 100m**, he could challenge for gold, but right now, he’s **behind the specialists**.  

#### **6. Emmanuel Eseme (CMR) – 10.02**  
- **Why 6th?** Eseme is **solid but not elite**. His **9.98 (+0.3) in Paris** was a standout, but most of his races are **10.0x**. He lacks the **top-tier explosiveness** of the favorites.

### **Final Thoughts:**  
- **Thompson** is the **clear favorite** based on **recent dominance**.  
- **Coleman** will challenge early but **fade late**.  
- **Omanyala** is **too inconsistent** to win but **could surprise** if he nails the start.  
- **Simbine & Tebogo** will be **close but not enough** for the podium.  
- The rest are **just filling lanes**.  

**Predicted Race:** Thompson blasts out, Coleman leads at 50m, but Thompson surges late. Omanyala closes hard but falls just short. Simbine and Tebogo battle for 4th.
